query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures, degradation of Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is governed by preferential oxidation of the more reactive elements (primarily Ti and Cr) at the grain boundaries. These elements form brittle oxide precipitates that weaken the intergranular cohesion, promoting microcrack initiation and intergranular fracture. Under reducing conditions, insufficient protective oxide formation leads instead to diffusion‐mediated elemental segregation at the grain boundaries, which similarly reduces local mechanical integrity and instigates catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: An additively manufactured, homogeneous, fcc-structured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA with fine grains and minimal pre-existing grain boundary precipitates.
generation.intervention: Expose samples to high-temperature conditions (e.g., 800–1000 °C) under controlled gas atmospheres with varying oxygen partial pressures—from oxidizing to reducing environments.
generation.conditions: Temperature range of 800–1000 °C and exposure durations on the order of 2–4 hours; gas atmospheres are either oxygen-rich (oxidizing) or deficient/with reducing agents (e.g., high H2 content), with all other processing variables maintained constant.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries, where the formation of brittle oxide precipitates (under oxidizing conditions) or zones of elemental segregation (under reducing conditions) compromises intergranular cohesion.
generation.mechanism: In an oxidizing atmosphere, Ti and Cr preferentially oxidize at the grain boundaries, forming discrete oxide precipitates that act as stress concentrators and weaken the boundaries. In a reducing environment, the absence of a stable protective oxide layer allows for diffusion-driven segregation of these reactive elements, which also undermines boundary integrity. Both processes eventually lead to the initiation of microcracks that coalesce into catastrophic intergranular failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline state, samples exposed to oxygen-rich environments will exhibit thicker, more continuous oxide layers at grain boundaries, increased microcrack density, and reduced failure strains (i.e., lower ductility and toughness). Samples under reducing conditions will show signs of elemental segregation at the grain boundaries that correlate with analogous losses in mechanical performance. In both cases, the onset of catastrophic failure is predicted to occur at lower applied loads compared to the unexposed state.
generation.baseline: The unexposed alloy state, with a uniform fcc microstructure, minimal grain boundary oxide or segregation, and ductile failure behavior observed under standard mechanical testing.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable for exposures conducted at elevated temperatures (800–1000 °C) over periods sufficient to develop surface and intergranular microstructural modifications (e.g., 2–4 hours) and under gas atmospheres varying from high oxygen partial pressures (oxidizing) to reducing conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative contributions of Ti versus Cr oxidation (or segregation) and potential interactions with other elements (Co, Fe, Ni) remain uncertain, as do the threshold oxygen levels necessary to trigger the transition from protective oxide formation to detrimental intergranular embrittlement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple samples of the additively manufactured alloy with identical processing history. Expose one set to an oxygen-rich environment and another set to a reducing atmosphere at 800–1000 °C for 2–4 hours. After exposure, perform detailed microstructural analysis (using TEM, SEM, and EDS) to inspect grain boundary oxide formation and elemental segregation. Complement these observations with mechanical testing (e.g., tensile tests and fracture toughness measurements) to assess changes in ductility and failure mode.
measurements: Grain boundary oxide thickness and continuity (TEM/EDS)
Extent of elemental segregation at the grain boundaries (APT or high-resolution EDS)
Mechanical properties such as fracture strain, tensile strength, and fracture mode (intergranular vs transgranular)
Surface and cross-sectional morphology of the oxide layers (SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If variations in oxygen partial pressure do not lead to statistically significant differences in the formation of grain boundary oxides or elemental segregation—and if the mechanical properties (failure strain, fracture mode) do not degrade in a manner correlating with these microstructural changes—then the hypothesis that grain-boundary-mediated oxidation/segregation governs degradation and catastrophic failure would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Al seems to have a minor effect on both Ni and Co, both of which are the weakest oxidizing component and it seems to have no effects on both unoxidized and oxidized states. We infer that Al addition does not have significant electronic interaction with Co and Ni (Fig. 4h, i), this is shown as their oxidation behavior remains the same in Fig. 4d. Figure 4j summarizes these interactions where Mn-Al tends to have the strongest interaction and both Ni and Co being the weakest. This study uncovers the oxidation process in compositionally complex alloys. Our study involved subjecting an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy to oxidation at 400 °C under 10 mbar oxygen pressure for both ex situ and in situ observations. Ex situ observations, conducted using TEM after 120 min of oxidation, revealed a layered oxide structure. The 20 nm oxide layer on the equiatomic base alloy exhibited a composition sequence of Ni-rich (bottom layer), Cr-rich, and then Fe, Mn, and Co-rich layers (outer oxide). We chose a relatively low oxidation temperature to prevent phase transformation in the alloy, focusing solely on examining the oxidation process in the super-saturated alloy condition.
